original_note: Title "Timbangan sa Bukal" for "Spring Balance": in Cebuano bukal = TO BOIL (this same batch uses it that way three times — pagbukal/nagbukal/mobukal sa tubig), and a water spring is tubod (used correctly in ffct-25532's title "Mainit nga Tubod"). Bukal is never a mechanical coil spring in either language. The card's OWN body and emph_bis use the right word, "tinggol" — the title is the outlier, reading as "boiling scale".
fact_en:
How does a spring balance measure weight?

A heavier object stretches the spring inside it more! This stretching is how it measures weight.
fact_bis:
Unsaon pagsukod sa kabug-aton sa spring balance?

Ang mas bug-at nga butang mas mobira sa tinggol sa sulod niini! Mao ni kini nga nagsukod sa kabug-aton.

original_note: "Metals like iron" becomes "Ang mga metal sama sa BAKAL" — bakal = TO BUY in Cebuano (iron is puthaw); it is on the confirmed false-friend list for this corpus. The clause reads as "metals such as buying", and the card's named exemplar of a metal is destroyed with no correction anywhere in the card (it only says "metal" and "metal nga kutsara"). Lower severity than the others since the headline fact (metals heat fast) survives; flagged because it is a confirmed swap and the card never supplies puthaw. Note ffct-25451 has the same word ("pabrika sa bakal" for steel factories) but there it is a
fact_en: Metals like iron have low specific heat capacity, so they heat up quickly with little energy. That's why a metal spoon in soup gets hot fast!
fact_bis: Ang mga metal sama sa bakal adunay ubos nga specific heat capacity, kay dali silang maginit sa gamayng enerhiya. Mao nang ang metal nga kutsara sa sopas modali og mainit!

original_note: title_bis "Tunog Bakal 15 Beses" for "Sound Steel 15x Faster". bakal in Cebuano = TO BUY (Tagalog bakal = iron/steel; Cebuano is puthaw / asero) — a confirmed false friend in this corpus. The title is the outlier: this card's own body keeps "steel" in English, and ffct-27473 in the same batch correctly uses "puthaw".
fact_en:
Why does sound travel faster in steel than in air?

Sound travels about fifteen times faster in steel! Particles in solids are packed closer together, so they pass vibrations more quickly.
fact_bis:
Ngano mas paspas ang tunog sa steel kaysa sa hangin?

Mga napulo-limang beses nga mas paspas ang tunog sa steel! Mas duol ang mga particle sa solid, mao nga mas paspas mo-pass sa vibrations.

original_note: title_bis "Magnet Nickel Cobalt Bakal" uses bakal for the iron of "Magnets Pull Nickel Cobalt Too". Again bakal = to buy in Cebuano, not iron (puthaw). Body evidence that the title is the outlier: this card's body writes "iron" in English and the parallel card ffct-27473 writes "Dili lang puthaw ang gidani sa mga magnet".
fact_en: Did you know permanent magnets don't just attract iron? They also strongly pull in nickel and cobalt metals!
fact_bis: Nahibaw-an ba ka nga ang permanent magnets dili lang makadani og iron? Kusog sad nila makadani og nickel ug cobalt metals!

original_note: "Magnet & Nail" / "iron nail" becomes "bakal nga pako" in BOTH the title_bis ("Magnet ug Pako") and the body (twice). In Cebuano pako = WING (nail is lansang), and bakal = TO BUY (iron is puthaw — this same batch uses puthaw correctly in ffct-27958 and ffct-27998). Nothing in the card restores it, so the child reads "what happens when a magnet comes near a buy-wing" and never learns the object is an iron nail. The whole probe (magnetic domains in iron) is unanswerable.
fact_en:
What happens when a magnet gets close to an iron nail?

When a magnet is brought near an unmagnetized iron nail, the nail's internal magnetic domains temporarily align to attract the magnet!
fact_bis:
Unsay mahitabo kung moduol ang magnet sa bakal nga pako?

Kung duol ang magnet sa bakal nga pako nga wala’y magnet, temporaryo nga mag-uyon ang mga magnetic domains sulod sa pako aron makadani sa magnet!

original_note: "gikan sa nabulok nga mga tanom ug hayop" uses bulok, which in Cebuano means COLOUR (and dull-witted), not rotten — that is Tagalog. Correct Cebuano is nadunot/nalata (the card's own terms list has madunot). Nothing else in the Cebuano supplies the decay idea, so the source of soil carbon (decayed plants and animals) is lost.
fact_en: Soil stores lots of carbon from rotting plants and animals! Believe it or not, there is even more carbon in the soil than in the air.
fact_bis: Ang yuta magtipig og daghang carbon gikan sa nabulok nga mga tanom ug hayop! Mas daghan pa gani ang carbon sa yuta kaysa sa hangin.

original_note: "gibulok sila sa decomposer sama sa bakterya ug fungi" — bulok = COLOUR in Cebuano (Tagalog false friend for rotten/decayed); correct is gidunot/gilata/gadugmok. This is the card's only verb for "break them down", and no other Cebuano word in the card restores it, so the decomposition mechanism itself is not stated in Cebuano. The terms list carries the correct madunot.
fact_en: When plants and animals die, decomposers like bacteria and fungi break them down, returning carbon to the soil and air as carbon dioxide!
fact_bis: Kung mamatay ang tanom ug hayop, gibulok sila sa decomposer sama sa bakterya ug fungi, nga nagbalik sa carbon sa yuta ug hangin isip carbon dioxide!

original_note: Tagalog false friend in the body's central comparison. EN: "Why do some hot springs smell like rotten eggs?" BIS: "Ngano ang ubang hot spring mobaho sama sa BULOK nga itlog?" In Cebuano bulok = COLOUR (unsa'y bulok sa imong sinina?); rotten egg is bugok nga itlog (general rot = dunot/lata). The card reads "smells like a coloured egg", and nothing in the card restores "rotten" — the answer only says the water picks up the smell from sulfur-rich rocks. The whole point of the card is the rotten-egg smell cue for sulfur, so a Cebuano-only child loses the fact the card depends on. Note the corpus u
fact_en:
Why do some hot springs smell like rotten eggs?

It’s because of sulfur gas! As the water travels underground, it passes through sulfur-rich rocks, picking up that distinct rotten egg smell along the way.
fact_bis:
Ngano ang ubang hot spring mobaho sama sa bulok nga itlog?

Tungod kini sa sulfur gas! Samtang moagi ang tubig sa ilalom sa yuta, moagi kini sa mga bato nga adunay sulfur, mao nga makuha niini ang baho.

original_note: title_bis "Hinaw nga Tubig sa Bukal" for "Clear Spring Water". Classic Tagalog false friend: TL bukal = spring, but Cebuano bukal = to BOIL (pabukala ang tubig); a water source is tuburan — which this card's OWN body uses correctly ("pag mogawas sa tuburan"), the strongest sign the title is the outlier. Compounding it, "hinaw" is hand-washing water in Cebuano, not "clear" (tin-aw). The title reads "wash-water from the boiling" — a different thing from clear spring water, and it is never corrected in the title's own terms.
fact_en: Rain soaks into the ground and collects underneath. It passes through rocks and sand, so when it comes out at a spring, the water is clear!
fact_bis: Mosulod ang ulan sa yuta ug matipon sa ilalom. Moagi kini sa mga bato ug balas, mao nga limpyo ang tubig pag mogawas sa tuburan!

original_note: bis: "sulfur gas nga baho og bulok nga itlog" for EN "smells like rotten eggs". In Cebuano bulok = COLOUR (rotten is dunot/lata); this is the confirmed Tagalog false friend. The card's whole identifying hook is the rotten-egg smell and nothing in the card restores it — terms even carry 'rotten egg'/'amoy itlog' but the body never says dunot. A Cebuano-only reader gets 'smells like a coloured egg' and cannot answer what sulfur gas smells like.
fact_en: Active volcanoes release sulfur gas that smells like rotten eggs! When this gas suddenly increases, it means the magma inside may be heating up.
fact_bis: Ang aktibong bulkan mogawas og sulfur gas nga baho og bulok nga itlog! Kung kalit nga modaghan kini, pasabot nag-init ang magma sa sulod.

original_note: title_bis "Soapstone Marka Bakal" uses bakal for "Metal" (title_en: Talc Marks Metal Factories). bakal in Cebuano = TO BUY; iron/metal is puthaw — the card's own body says "Unsaon pagmarka sa puthaw" and "marka sa puthaw". Title reads as "soapstone mark buy", so the metal-marking subject is gone from the title.
fact_en:
How do factory workers draw clear marks on metal for welding?

They use Talc or soapstone shaped like a pencil! It leaves a clear white mark on metal because the soft Talc rubs off easily.
fact_bis:
Unsaon pagmarka sa puthaw sa mga trabahador sa pabrika para sa welding?

Mogamit sila og Talc o soapstone nga porma sa lapis! Mibilin kini og tin-aw nga puti nga marka sa puthaw kay sayon ra makalmot ang humok nga Talc.
